problem: Prior VLN agents, mostly RL-based sequential local-decision policies, ignore the spatial route prior inherent in VLN data (shortest paths in R2R, a few concatenated shortest sub-paths in R4R/RxR). They face an exponentially large path space and make only local decisions, and their success rate has plateaued around 62% single-run and 73% beam-search on R2R val-unseen.
motivation: Human instructors tend to describe shortest routes, or routes made of a few local shortest sub-paths. Given an origin and destination, the route is then essentially determined. The authors measure that R4R/RxR routes decompose into far fewer shortest sub-paths than random routes (ratio about 0.21 and 0.25 vs 0.79), so the prior is a general property of VLN rather than a dataset bias. Exploiting it turns navigation into global classification over candidate destinations.
key_idea: Exploit the shortest-path / composed-shortest-subpath route prior to recast VLN as classification over destination nodes (or a sequential classification over shortest sub-paths) on a known or on-the-fly explored sub-graph.
insight: Most of the gain comes from the prior and the global path-level scoring, not from better exploration: the same Follower alone gets only 0.39 SR on R2R val-unseen (0.58 with the Speaker) versus 0.73 (0.78 with the Speaker) for the proposed model on the same explored graph. Ablations show that Aggr_soft beats a plain MLP on R4R (CLS 0.61 vs 0.58 with a known map), that gains grow with explored sub-graph size (40 nodes is a good trade-off), and that neighboring score aggregation hurts on tiny sub-graphs (10 nodes) but helps at 20 nodes or more. The small val-seen to val-unseen gap suggests the approach overfits less than RL agents.
method: Shortest-path classification: with a known map and shortest-path prior, the route is determined by (start, destination), so VLN becomes argmax over all nodes of F(path, instruction), where F is a dual-LSTM (path and instruction encoders, concatenated final states, MLP) trained with cross-entropy.
Neighboring score aggregation: at inference, the scores of a node and all nodes within 3 m are summed before the argmax, matching the SR success radius.
Route decomposition (Algorithm 1): greedily split any ground-truth route into a minimal number of consecutive local shortest sub-paths (about 3.3 on average in R4R vs about 12 steps).

Sequential-decision variant: the agent runs K rounds, each classifying the next end node of a shortest sub-path from the current node, with a learned Stop candidate. It is trained with IL (teacher forcing) plus RL using a CLS reward.

Progress-aware scoring: MLP([h^I_j, h^P_last]) is computed for every instruction step j and aggregated by log-sum-exp (soft-DTW-like soft max), so partial paths are matched to the right instruction progress.

Explore-and-exploit for unknown maps: a Follower agent runs state-factored beam search to collect about 40 visited nodes as a sub-graph, then the classification or sequential model picks the best route on that sub-graph. Known-map variant: DFS over the whole graph.
Optional ensembling with a Speaker model (+spk) to rescore candidates.

results: With about 40 explored nodes, the single model reaches 73% SR on R2R val-unseen (74% with a known map) and 78% with a Speaker ensemble, outperforming the 3-model ensembled VLN-BERT (74%) without pretraining. On R4R val-unseen it beats single-run methods on SR/CLS/nDTW (CLS 0.60 vs SSM 0.53), although this comparison is unfair because of the extra exploration. It also generalizes better from seen to unseen, but has worse NE than several baselines.
limitations: Classification errors cause large deviations from the goal, giving worse navigation error than several RL agents.
Requires an extra exploration phase (or full-map DFS) with very long total trajectory lengths; SPL on the leaderboard is about 0.01–0.02 when exploration is counted.
Relies on the route prior, which needs sub-graph coverage of the GT route. The neighbor aggregation is inexact on incomplete graphs and is skipped for R4R.
